newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hanover Re to take part in California quake cover.
newsitem.headline: Hanover Re to take part in California quake cover.

text.p: German reinsurer Hannover Re is participating with $50 million dollars in the reinsurance coverage for the California Earthquake Authority (CEA), the company told Reuters.
The total open market reinsurance for the programme runs to $2.0 billion.
"Our premium income from this business will amount to 10 million marks ($6.6 million)," Hannover Re chief executive Wilhelm Zeller said.
"We are already participating in a similar programme in Hawaii. In Florida, moves are underway to install such a scheme for hurricane losses."
The price offered by CEA had been "very attractive," Zeller said. "The CEA pool will have a beneficial effect on the overall reinsurance pricing for California earthquake reinsurance," Zeller said.
At present, insurance companies selling property cover to California home-owners are obliged to offer a quake endorsement. For that reason, many insurers left the market or reduced their exposure.
From 1 January 1997, the CEA pool, managed by the state of California, will provide earthquake cover to private individuals, thus relieving individual property insurers.
However, the cover carries high deductibles.

Policyholders will only be reimbursed if the loss amounts to more than 15 percent of the insured value. For a house with a value of $300,000, the insured has to pay the first $45,000 in the event of a loss.
Prices are not low for this cover, they run to 0.3 percent or close to $1,000 for a $300,000 house, Hannover Re said.
The CEA pools offers up to $10.5 billion cover, most of it provided by U.S. insurers, Zeller said. Two billion dollars were placed in open international reinsurance markets.
"We and other reinsurers will have to pay these two billion dollars if the total loss from one quake exceeds four billion dollars," Zeller said.

The highest loss from an earthquake in California so far was recorded in January 1994, when a quake measuring 6.8 on the Mercali scale hit the Los Angeles area and caused losses of $13.3 billion, most of it in the Northridge region, Hannover Re said.
